title: Luke close: great joy (Luke 24:50–53)
hookLine: he blesses them with lifted hands; they return with great joy and are always in the temple
tomorrow: in the beginning was the Word

cards: Ninety days ago, Luke's Gospel opened in the temple in Jerusalem. An old priest named Zechariah was burning incense, and an angel told him he'd have a son.
He didn't believe it, and he came out of the sanctuary unable to speak. The people outside were waiting for him, and he could only make signs with his hands.
Today, on the last page, Luke finishes the sentence he started on the first.

teach.h: HE LIFTED UP HIS HANDS, AND BLESSED.
teach.b: Luke's last four verses, in the King James words: "And he led them out as far as to Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven. And they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy: And were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God."
Lifted hands. In Leviticus, Aaron the priest lifts up his hands toward the people and blesses them.

teach.h: A SPEECHLESS PRIEST; NOW A BLESSING.
teach.b: Some readers see Luke closing a circle: a Gospel that opened with a priest who came out speechless ends with Jesus blessing his friends with his hands raised, still blessing as he's taken up. Then the joy.
Not long before, these same people were frightened, grieving, calling the women's news idle tales.
Now he's gone from their sight, and they go back with great joy, in the temple every day, praising God.

teach.h: BEGUN IN THE TEMPLE, ENDED THERE.
teach.b: Luke started in the temple, and he ends there. Look back over these ninety days. Zechariah and Elizabeth.
Mary's song. Shepherds on the night shift. Simeon holding the child.
The sermon at Nazareth. The good Samaritan. The lost sheep, the lost coin, the lost son.
Zacchaeus in the tree. The widow's two coins. The upper room, the garden, the look across the courtyard, a criminal promised paradise, bread broken at Emmaus.
Luke said at the start he was writing so his reader would know these things were certain.

teach.h: RETURNED TO JERUSALEM WITH GREAT JOY.
teach.b: He ends not with an argument, but with joy, and blessing, and people praising God.

how: Christians celebrate the Ascension forty days after Easter, and in some churches services end the way Luke's Gospel does, with a minister lifting hands to bless the people.

games.q: you've walked out to Bethany with the risen Jesus. he lifts his hands, and while he's blessing you, he's taken up from your sight. what do you do?
o: stay on the hill, waiting for him to come back.
scatter and go home to Galilee.
worship him and go back to Jerusalem with great joy.
games.why: "they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy: and were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God."

practice: If you can, lift your hands a little, palms out or up, and bring the people in your life to mind one at a time: someone at home, someone at work, someone far away, someone you're struggling with.

As each one comes, wish them good: peace, rest, joy. If you pray, you can use the old blessing from the book of Numbers, The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; if you don't, simply hold them in good will.

wordCard.voice: Luke close. The end of Luke's Gospel: Jesus blessing his friends with lifted hands, and the friends going home with great joy, praising God in the temple.

orig.note: Greek: he blessed, literally spoke well of. from the same root as the English word eulogy.

carryVoice: Your line: with great joy. Tomorrow, a new Gospel: John, starting before the beginning. Ninety days of Luke, done.
